2: Your Conditional Access policies already require a compliant device.
That's only as good as Intune's compliance records, and by default, a device with no compliance policy assigned counts as compliant.

4: Here are six of Book 05's questions with the Intune A P I that answers each.
Enrolled devices, with their OS, compliance state, encryption and last sync, come from managed devices, with the managed devices read permission.
Compliance policies, their assignments and their per-device statuses need the configuration read permission, in version one point oh.
The Settings Catalog and endpoint security policies, and assignment filters, use the same permission, but they're beta only.
Autopilot registrations are in version one point oh with the service configuration read permission, but whether each one has been given a deployment profile is beta only.
And every Intune A P I in Graph needs an active Intune license for the tenant.
5: Microsoft supports the Intune beta A P I's, but says they're subject to more frequent change, and recommends version one point oh where it can be used.
Three things the program relies on are beta-only today.
The Settings Catalog: Book 05's policy library is mostly Settings Catalog profiles, so exporting the library as code depends on beta.
Assignment filters: the filter list is beta, and version one point oh can't tell you which filter an assignment uses, which is why the validation kit's filter check needs its include-beta switch.
And Autopilot profiles: version one point oh lists registrations, but the profile assignment status and the profiles themselves are beta.
As design guidance, re-run a beta-dependent check after each beta change before you use its result as evidence.
6: A managed device is Intune's record of an enrolled device.

The checks read its compliance state, one of seven values from compliant to in grace period; its last successful sync; its OS version and encryption status; and its Entra device I D, the join key to the Entra device object.
The same record also returns a person's name, email address and phone number.
The checks name only what they need in select and leave those out, so a check's output never carries a person's name or address.
And watch for defaults that look like data: some properties, such as the MAC address and physical memory, return default values when you list devices.
Their real values come only from reading one device and selecting them.
7: A compliance policy's assignments list its targets.
In version one point oh a group target carries a group I D, and beta documents an exclusion target.
A policy with no assignments, or with only exclusions, applies to no device, and remember, by default an unassigned device counts as compliant.
Each policy's device statuses give one row per device, with a status such as non-compliant, error or conflict.
But the row carries a device name, and its I D is described only as the key of the entity, not as the managed device's I D.
So the checks join status rows to devices on the name, and flag names held by more than one device.
That's an inference, and an open review item.
Two tenant-wide settings sit above every policy; their read permission wasn't confirmed on Learn, so the checks don't read them.
8: Two things look useful and don't belong in a read-only collector.
Remote actions: retire, wipe and even sync device all need the privileged operations permission, delegated or application.
A collector that holds it could wipe the fleet, so as design guidance, keep it in a separate pipeline with its own approval step.
And report export jobs: creating one needs a read-write permission, with no read-only option listed, and the file it produces sits on blob storage behind a signed address, not on the Graph host.
The example client won't send its token anywhere else.
So the checks page through the list A P I's instead.
A hundred policies cost about two hundred and one requests, well under Intune's limit of a thousand per twenty seconds per app per tenant.
9: Noncompliant devices lists devices that are noncompliant, in grace, in error or in conflict, with the failing policies.
Compliance coverage lists policies with no assignment or only exclusions, and devices no policy reports on.
Stale check-in lists devices with no Intune sync inside the fourteen-day validity period or the ninety-day cleanup age, or none at all.
Device posture lists Windows and Mac devices not reporting encryption, and devices below the OS floor.
And Autopilot profiles, on beta, lists registrations whose profile isn't assigned and in sync.
Every control they evidence is in the nist Moderate baseline: configuration settings, the baseline, the inventory, encryption, and flaw remediation.
The mapping is the program's reading; the assessor decides.
The permissions are a reader's set.
10: Lab 1 runs each check against a fictional fleet of nine devices and six Autopilot registrations.
Two policies reach no device: the kiosk policy has only an exclusion, and an old Mac pilot has no assignment at all.
Two devices, a kiosk and a Mac, have no policy reporting on them, so with the tenant's default setting they count as compliant.
And W S zero zero zero two is flagged as ambiguous: two devices share that name, so a status row could belong to either.
Step six asks the client to read the Autopilot collection as a G C C High run would.
It returns not available, with the reason, and makes no request, because the call list follows Intune's government service description, not the A P I page.

11: Lab 2 runs the checks read-only against your own test tenant, worldwide or G C C, never production, with an Intune license and a few enrolled test devices.
Register one app in the tenant's own cloud, with a certificate.
Grant only the read permissions for the checks you run, and never the privileged operations permission.
Run each task in Python, or connect in PowerShell and run it there; a missing permission stops the run before any Graph call.
Compare the results with the Intune admin center's compliance, device and Autopilot views, and record the module's open review items, such as whether a status row's I D matches a managed device.
Then back it out: remove the permissions, delete the app registration and its certificate, and delete the saved results, which hold device names and serial numbers.
12: Book 05's agency manages Windows with Group Policy, and often Configuration Manager, and is moving to Intune in a G C C tenant.
G C C has no separate Intune instance.
In Microsoft's words, G C C is the same instance as Intune in the commercial space, and it uses the worldwide Graph host.
G C C High and D O D share a separate government instance, with their own Graph hosts, and moving between instances means unenrolling and re-enrolling every device.

Microsoft's service description lists what isn't available there, with no plans to add it: Windows Autopilot, Remediations, feature update and compatibility reports, the ServiceNow connector and Subscription Activation.
Standard device management, compliance, configuration and app policies, is available, with Log Analytics export and Defender security settings management.
13: The Graph reference pages for Autopilot device identities list the A P I in the G C C High and D O D clouds, while Intune's service description lists Windows Autopilot as not available there.
The service description decides whether the feature can be used; an endpoint that answers doesn't make the feature supported.
That's an inference, and the kit's call list follows the stricter statement, so the Autopilot check is for G C C and commercial tenants.
The interim paths: run compliance coverage until it lists nothing, then change the tenant's default to not compliant.
Devices still on Group Policy aren't in Intune yet, so track them with the validation kit's platform inventory.
In G C C High or D O D, Book 05's Chapter 04 compares Autopilot device preparation.
And label the Settings Catalog export as beta.
14: Every control the checks evidence is in the nist special publication eight hundred fifty-three Moderate baseline: configuration baseline and settings, the component inventory, protection of information at rest and encryption on mobile devices, and flaw remediation for the OS floor.
Through Entra I D, compliance is the device-level signal that M twenty-two oh-nine asks agencies to consider when authorizing users, and that ScubaGear's managed-device policy relies on.
ScubaGear has no Intune baseline of its own.
Book 11's Appendix A has the M twenty-two oh-nine mapping, and Book 05's Chapter 10 says what an assessor reads.

The evidence an I S S O keeps: each check's dated output, with its evidences list and the beta label; the coverage result and the changed default; and encryption findings confirmed in Intune's own report.
